candidates.name: C1. Chatarreras register and monthly forms kit (Ley sobre Comercialización y Procesamiento de Materiales Metálicos)
candidates.trigger: Decreto 61-2014, La Gaceta 33,614. Art. 2: obligatory municipal registry. coverage.category: 1. Household employers: domestic workers, live-in carers, nannies
coverage.found: Reglamento del IHSS says domestic workers are exempt from compulsory social insurance until conditions are set (https://www.tsc.gob.hn/web/leyes/Reglamento_de_Apliación_de_Ley_IHSS.pdf); only an old (2006) voluntary annual-fee programme was found. No clear mandatory household-employer filing. Weak.

coverage.category: 2. Scrap-metal dealers
coverage.found: Decreto 61-2014 (La Gaceta 33,614, 23 Dec 2014) requires municipal registration, a special operations register (purchases with seller ID/origin/weight/value, sales, exports, recycling), per-load guide and certificate of origin on protected forms, and monthly copies of forms to the municipality. Fines 1-5 monthly minimum wages, 3-month suspension, then cancellation. New candidate C1.

coverage.category: 3. Second-hand dealers and pawnbrokers
coverage.found: Casas de empeño are 'convocado SI' in the CNBS/URMOPRELAFT APNFD list (also prestamistas no bancarios, antiques/art/luxury goods dealers). This is the same buyer group and duty as K01. Nothing new beyond K01.

coverage.category: 4. Gold and jewellery buyers
coverage.found: Precious-metals and jewellery buy/sell/manufacture is 'convocado SI' in the APNFD list (sector 7). Nothing new beyond K01.

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: No Honduran dismantler regime found. Used-car dealers are APNFD convocado SI (K01). Only abandoned-vehicle seizure news in Tegucigalpa (DNVT/AMDC, 280 vehicles). Nothing new.

coverage.category: 6. Livestock traders, markets and animal transport
coverage.found: Bovine movement needs GUIASA (in force 1 Oct 2020), fierro certification and carta de venta/Boleta de Venta Pecuaria under the PCM 032-2018 traceability system. SENASA runs the Trazar-Agro platform (143,253 people and 148,726 establishments registered). Candidate C4, with a state tool already in place.

coverage.category: 7. Small abattoirs and butchers
coverage.found: SENASA inspects municipal rastros. ARSA gives sanitary licences (2/4/6-year terms) and closes butchers and food processors. No dedicated butcher-register duty found. Candidate C5 (weak).

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: No Honduran beekeeper registry or reporting duty found. Honey is mostly for own consumption. Nothing.

coverage.category: 9. Veterinary practices and veterinary medicine sellers
coverage.found: The RTCA 65.05.51 and 65.05.52 regional rules and the SENASA Ley Fitozoosanitaria govern vet-medicine establishments, but the regente duties could not be confirmed. Close to K03 (agroservicios regente file). Nothing new beyond K03.

coverage.category: 10. Well drillers and water abstraction
coverage.found: Only the Ley General de Aguas and municipal permits for drilling/exploration (Siguatepeque regulation) were found. No driller register or periodic duty confirmed. Nothing new.

coverage.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers
coverage.found: No search spent here (budget went to other categories). Only incidental: municipal rules for chatarras as 'residuos especiales'.

coverage.category: 12. Lift, boiler and pressure-equipment owners and inspectors
coverage.found: One search found no Honduran lift or boiler inspection regime; results were from Argentina, Mexico and Puerto Rico. The STSS occupational safety certification of companies exists, but it is not equipment-specific. Nothing found (unverified).

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: JAAs must register with ERSAPS and file annual technical and financial reports by 30 April. Candidate C2.

coverage.category: 14. Pesticide and fertiliser dealers and applicators
coverage.found: No search spent here. Treated as K03 (agroservicios SENASA file). Nothing new.

coverage.category: 15. Labour contractors and recruitment agencies
coverage.found: Private employment agencies are registered by the STSS Dirección General de Empleo (Decreto 32-2003, Acuerdo STSS-141-2015). Recruiters for work abroad need a Certificado de Operatividad. A small, niche group. Candidate C7 (weak).

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: No Honduran rule on funeral homes or cemeteries found. ARSA's published acuerdos concern lodging and recreation. Nothing.

coverage.category: 17. Community and religious bodies: associations, charities, halal and kosher supervision
coverage.found: Asociaciones civiles and ONGD under Gobernación/URSAC are obliged to present information (statutes, reforms, board elections). The Ley ONG-D is from 2011 and its reglamento from 2013. The exact periodic duty was not confirmed. Candidate C6 (unverified). Halal and kosher: nothing.

coverage.category: 18. Transport operators: minibus, taxi, moto-taxi, small trucking and bus fleets
coverage.found: IHTT started a mototaxi census clean-up on 28 Sep 2026. Municipal authorisations do not replace the IHTT Permiso de Explotación or Certificado de Operación. Related to K04. Candidate C3 (the page fetch was blocked, so details unverified).

coverage.category: 19. Market traders, street vendors, money changers
coverage.found: BCH Acuerdo 01/2026 (La Gaceta 37,078, 24 Feb 2026) says only the BCH and habilitated exchange agents may trade foreign currency. The content was not read. No vendor or market regime found. Candidate C8 (unverified).

coverage.category: 20. Small licensed premises with inspections: tattoo studios, driving schools, childminders and nurseries, small food producers, hunting outfitters
coverage.found: ARSA licences for food premises have terms of 2/4/6 years, with closures reported (C5). Driving schools sit under IHTT/ENTT accreditation (Decreto 118-2021) with no register found. Childcare regulation is fragmented across CONEANFO, DINAF and STSS. No tattoo or hunting rules found.

coverage.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers
coverage.found: Thin, mostly negative. (a) No Honduran rule found on septic or fecal-sludge desludging, tanker permits, portable toilets or a haulers' register; the discharge rule is Acuerdo 058-96 (wastewater to water bodies and sewers, in force since 13 Dec 1997; Ley General de Aguas 181-2009 requires treating effluent), and no source links it to a desludger licence. Desludging is probably informal and municipal (sludge studies for Tegucigalpa date from 2012-2015). (b) Solid-waste haulers: the framework is Acuerdo Ejecutivo 1567-2010 (Reglamento de Gestión Integral de Residuos Sólidos, La Gaceta 32.449, 22 Feb 2011, not repealed per FAOLEX); I could not read its articles on hauler licensing. Municipalities run collection and set fees in each Plan de Arbitrios; small scrap yards get municipal operating permits, bigger processors need an environmental licence (El Heraldo, 2019). (c) New triggers: a Ley de Residuos Sólidos passed first debate (La Tribuna, 22 Jul 2026) and would require a regulation coordinated by MiAmbiente; the text is not available. UNDP/GEF (Mar 2025) supported three drafted regulations (SQUI, REPEL, RESIC), whose publication status I could not confirm. (d) Healthcare waste: Acuerdo 07-2008 covers infectious waste; hospitals and clinics pay private or municipal haulers (Tegucigalpa charged L330 a month per health unit in 2014 and suspended collection over unpaid fees). Nothing new beyond the incidental scrap-yard rule. Unchecked: the full text of Acuerdo 1567-2010, whether REPEL is in La Gaceta, the second debate of the waste law, and the Tegucigalpa/San Pedro Sula plan de arbitrios. Both WebFetch calls were blocked (403), so I relied on the search summaries.

result.competitor: No Honduran or Central American software or service found for the chatarrera register or certificate-of-origin forms. The only scrap-control software found is generic, sold in Mexico on Mercado Libre (MXN 7,000-12,000), with unverified features. No state portal found. Paper municipal registers are likely.
result.duty: Decreto 61-2014, Ley sobre Comercialización y Procesamiento de Materiales Metálicos, La Gaceta 33,614 (23 Dec 2014), Honduran national law of public order. Confirmed: Art. 2 requires registration in a municipal register of metal traders and industrialists, integrated into a national registry. Unverified (scanned PDF, OCR failed): Art. 3 operations register, Art. 5 guides, certificates of origin and monthly copies, Art. 8 fines of 1-5 minimum wages and suspension. Found no amendment or reglamento, and no evidence of enforcement in practice. Recent municipal "chatarra" operations (SPS June 2025 under Plan de Arbitrios art. 277; AMDC Jan 2024) target sidewalks and abandoned vehicles, not dealer registers.
result.market: No registry count found. No official number of registered chatarreras in SPS or Tegucigalpa. La Prensa (undated) reports about 15,000 t/month of recycled metal exports. The likely market is in the low hundreds of dealers nationwide, mostly informal. not_reached: municipal register counts (would need SIELHO public-information requests).
result.reason: The duty is real. Decreto 61-2014 (La Gaceta 33,614, 23 Dec 2014) requires anyone who habitually trades, exports, stores or transports copper, aluminium, bronze or iron to register in each municipality's Registro Municipal, which feeds a national registry. Searches confirmed the decree and Art. 2. Arts. 3-8 (special register, protected forms, monthly copies, fines) could not be checked: both PDFs are scanned images. I found no amendment and no enforcement after 2014. Municipal "chatarra" operations target abandoned vehicles and sidewalks, not dealer registers. No Honduran software exists for this (only generic Mexican scrap software). Enforcement looks weak, dealers are informal and unlikely to pay, and the market is small, so the score is low.

result.competitor: No commercial software or service for Honduran RCBF filing found in Spanish searches; only law-firm and Big-4 alerts. The main risk is that the CNBS must build its own "procedimientos digitales para la inscripción", meaning a free state portal will do the core filing. Comparable regimes run on free state systems: Costa Rica's Banco Central registry and Panama's SSNF system, where resident-agent lawyers file and receive a certificate. A tool could only add the document, ownership-chain, reminder and multi-client layer for accountants. Whether the portal accepts filings by third parties or accountants, and whether it offers an API or bulk upload, is unknown.
result.duty: Real and in force. Decreto 127-2026 (Ley de Transparencia y Registro Centralizado de Beneficiarios Finales) was published in La Gaceta on 3 Jul 2026 and took effect on publication. Who must register: national and foreign mercantile companies in the Registro Mercantil, trusts, investment funds and mixed public companies. They must declare every natural person holding 25% or more, or exercising control. Deadlines: CNBS regulation and digital procedures within 60 days (EY says business days); registry enabled within 6 months. First filing: KPMG says within 4 months of the registry opening, La Prensa says up to 6 months after the CNBS act; sources disagree. New companies register within 1 month of creation. Annual update by 30 May. Changes reported within 10 business days of the following month. Bearer shares must be converted. Fines: 20 to 500 minimum salaries, doubled for repeat offences. As of 9 Oct 2026, no search found the CNBS regulation or an open registry. I could not read the decree PDF (the fetch returned raw binary), so the article numbers and the bearer-share deadline are unconfirmed.
result.market: No national count of active sociedades found. Partial figures: Cohep counted 14,955 new businesses in 2024 in Tegucigalpa and San Pedro Sula combined. Cámara de Comercio de Cortés reported 6,966 new businesses in 2024, of which 3,066 were sociedades and 3,900 individual traders. A 2022 report said 61% of companies formed online via CCIT were single-owner. The stock of sociedades is plausibly in the tens of thousands (rough estimate, not verified). Many are single-owner, for which filing is trivial.
result.reason: The duty is real, mandatory, carries heavy fines and creates a mass one-off deadline plus a 30 May annual update. But the CNBS regulation and portal are still unpublished as of Oct 2026, so the timing and the core workflow are uncertain. The core filing will very likely go through a free CNBS digital portal, as in Costa Rica and Panama. That leaves only a thin document, reminder and multi-client layer for accountants and notaries. Many companies are single-owner, which makes filing simple. The once-a-year duty limits recurring willingness to pay. Distribution through accountants is feasible. No competitor was found, but the product shape cannot be judged until the portal exists. Recheck once the CNBS regulation is out.
